South of Fitzroy Crossing. / • In disyllables and words longer than three syllables primary stress is initial. / • In trisyllables primary stress varies between initial and second. / • Secondary stress on alternates after the primary or on the penult. / ˈyapa 'child' ˈkaŋani or kaˈŋani 'carried' / ˈwalakuˌwanṯi 'sons' ˈnjantuˌkuṟaḻu 'his-SUBJ' / Hudson, J. & E. Richards (1969). The Phonology of Walmatjari. Oceanic Linguistics 8, pp. 171–189. [p. 686] — Chapter, p. 55 (general, not Walmajarri-specific): "The prototypical stress pattern for these languages places main stress on the first syllable and secondary stress on alternate syllables thereafter, but we do find some variations on this theme."

new_statements.relation_note: Same primary placement as the catalog (initial, catalog classification fixed-dominant, stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 10100 100100 1000100 10000100 (1 = a stressed syllable) from StressTyp2). It refines in two places the catalog's fixed pattern does not capture: (a) trisyllables vary between initial and second-syllable primary stress (catalog encodes 100 only); (b) secondary stress is variable, 'on alternates after the primary or on the penult', whereas the catalog rule puts a single secondary on the antepenult in words of 4-8 syllables (1010, 10100, 100100, 1000100, 10000100) — compatible with the 'alternates after the primary' reading for 4-5 syllable words but not…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable in disyllables and in words of four or more syllables; in trisyllables primary stress varies between the first and the second syllable (ˈkaŋani ~ kaˈŋani 'carried'). StressTyp code [I] = initial. The entry is a digest of Hudson & Richards 1969 (Oceanic Linguistics 8: 171-189), not primary fieldwork by Goedemans.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated explicitly but variable: 'Secondary stress on alternates after the primary or on the penult.' The two five-syllable examples show both options: ˈwalakuˌwanṯi 'sons' (secondary on the 4th = penult) vs ˈnjantuˌkuṟaḻu 'his-SUBJ' (secondary on the 3rd = alternate after the primary).
new_statements.exceptions: Trisyllables: primary stress varies between initial and second syllable (ˈkaŋani or kaˈŋani 'carried'). No weight or morphological conditioning is given for the variation.
new_statements.identity_note: The entry is headed 'Walmajarri; Walmatjari', located 'South of Fitzroy Crossing', classified Pama-Nyungan, South-West, Ngumbin, and rests on Hudson & Richards 1969; no dialect is distinguished. Note that the copy consulted named as the Goedemans chapter is in fact the entire 2010 De Gruyter volume (896 pp.); the Walmajarri statement is in the volume's StressTyp appendix (p. 686), which the chapter itself (pp. 55-85) does not repeat — the chapter never names Walmajarri. The parenthetical in the listed citation, '(Miriwung = language no. 51 on the stress map)', belongs to a different item (Miriwung, on the Arnhem Land map, Figure 1 p. 68ff.); Walmajarri is a Kimberley language and is not on that map.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The item lists only one work and it was opened with a quotation, so there were no silent or not-opened listed works to spot-check. As substitutes I spot-checked (a) the Goedemans chapter proper (PDF pages 60-120): no Walmajarri statement, confirming the compiler; (b) the on-disk Thieberger 1993 text : Walmajarri entry lines 8178-8390 contains no stress/accent/prominence term, and the general 'Word stress is usually on the first syllable' remark at p. 6 (line 826) is verbatim, as earlier passes. Not a listed work, not added, but noted for the record: the folder already holds Hammond 1994, 'An OT account of variability in Walmatjari stress', ROA-20, downloaded 2026-09-16 by an earlier reading…

readall_conflicts: Only one work was opened, so there is no disagreement between sources. The one tension is between the catalog's fully fixed rule string (trisyllables 100; a single secondary on the antepenult in longer words) and the StressTyp 2010 entry it descends from, which reports variation: trisyllables ˈkaŋani ~ kaˈŋani 'carried' (initial or second), and secondary stress 'on alternates after the primary or on the penult' (ˈwalakuˌwanṯi vs ˈnjantuˌkuṟaḻu). This is a hedge the catalog's pattern string flattens, not a different placement type; primary stress stays initial as the dominant pattern. Earlier passes logged in the same Thieberger 1993 p. 6, 'Word stress is usually on the first syllable' for WA languages in general; Blake 1991 not openable) are consistent with initial stress.

audit.reasoning: All deciding quotations check out verbatim in held text (Gordon 2002:509 + fn. 9 in refs/; Hammond 1994 pp. 4-5 in the ROA PDF, now saved durably; H&R 1976 p. c.73 in held), and the sole primary 6σ attestation (wálakuwàntilu = 100100) plus Gordon's explicit schemata support the catalog string over StressTyp2's penult coding, so nothing in hand suggests the dominant-register coding is wrong. But the classification is second-hand twice over: a 2002 typological survey reading an unheld 1978 grammar, and a 1994 OT paper reading an unheld 1969 phonology article. The primary data (via Hammond) show free variation at 3σ, three lexical classes each at 4σ and 5σ with no stated default, and no words of 7-8σ, so lengths 5 and 7-8 rest entirely on Gordon's paraphrase of Hudson 1978. sources.quote: From H&R 1969: disyllables initial; 'Trisyllabic words are stressed on either the first or second syllable'; quadrisyllables three lexical types (initial+penult secondary / fixed antepenult tjalánana / vacillating); five-syllable words three types (initial+penult wálakuwànti, initial+antepenult njántukùralu, vacillating); 'Only one six-syllabled word is cited and it has an initial main stress and antepenult secondary stress' (wálakuwàntilu).
